Mucosa.description: The mucosa is the moist lining covering the upper surface of the tongue. It is a stratified squamous epithelium, keratinised mainly over the filiform papillae and non-keratinised elsewhere, sitting on a basement membrane above a lamina propria of connective tissue that rises up into the papillae.
clinical: Most tongue cancers are squamous cell carcinomas that arise in this lining, and the side (lateral) border of the tongue is their most common site.

Papillae.description: Papillae are the small raised bumps on the top of the tongue, each with a core of connective tissue covered by epithelium. Filiform papillae are the most numerous and give the tongue its rough texture, but they have no taste buds. The other three types carry taste buds: fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped and scattered among the filiform papillae, foliate papillae are folds on the sides of the back of the tongue, and circumvallate papillae are large and sunk in a trench just in front of the V-shaped groove at the back.
clinical: A harmless condition in which patches of filiform papillae are lost, leaving smooth red areas that change shape and move over time.

When filiform papillae fail to shed their keratin, they can grow abnormally long and sometimes turn dark, a condition called hairy or black hairy tongue. Poor oral hygiene, smoking and some antibiotics are linked to it.

Taste buds.description: Taste buds are barrel-shaped clusters of cells that span the full thickness of the epithelium and open to the surface through a small taste pore. Receptor cells inside detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami tastes, and their microvilli (taste hairs) reach into the pore to meet dissolved food.
clinical: Damage to the chorda tympani, or to the facial nerve (VII) before it gives off the chorda, can reduce taste on the front two-thirds of the tongue on that side.

Intrinsic muscle.description: The intrinsic tongue muscles lie entirely inside the tongue, in four sets: superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse and vertical. They change the tongue's shape, for example by curling its tip, narrowing and lengthening it, or flattening it, and they are skeletal muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII). Thin sheets of connective tissue (perimysium) wrap the fibre bundles, with a little fat between them.
clinical: Long-standing damage to the hypoglossal nerve (XII) makes the tongue muscles on that side shrink (atrophy) and may cause visible twitching (fasciculation).

Glands.description: Von Ebner glands are small serous glands lying among the muscle fibres under the back papillae. Their watery secretion flows out through ducts into the trenches of the circumvallate papillae and the clefts of the foliate papillae, rinsing the taste pores so that food chemicals can keep reaching the taste buds.

Nerves & vessels.description: The tongue's nerves carry different signals: the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) supplies sensation and taste to the back third; the lingual nerve (V3) gives general sensation to the front two-thirds, while its taste fibres come from the facial nerve (VII) through the chorda tympani; and the hypoglossal nerve (XII) supplies the tongue's movement muscles. The lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid, supplies the tongue, and the deep lingual vein drains it.
clinical: The lingual nerve runs close to the lower wisdom teeth, so injury during their removal can numb the front two-thirds of the tongue on that side.
Damage to the hypoglossal nerve (XII) weakens the tongue on that side; when the tongue is pushed out it deviates toward the weak side, and speech and swallowing can be affected.

parts.description: Stratified squamous epithelium is the thick, many-layered lining of the dorsum of the tongue, made of flattened cells that resist abrasion from food. Over the filiform papillae and much of the dorsum it is keratinised, meaning its surface cells are hardened by the protein keratin, but it stays non-keratinised around the taste papillae and on the underside. In a section it appears as a pink sheet of many cell layers resting on the basement membrane.

The lamina propria is the layer of loose connective tissue lying directly beneath the surface epithelium. It contains small blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels, and on the tongue it rises up into the papillae as connective tissue cores that bring blood vessels close to the avascular epithelium. In a section it is the pale, fibrous layer with many small capillaries, lying between the epithelium and the deeper tissue.

Fungiform papillae are small, mushroom-shaped projections scattered over the front two-thirds of the dorsum of the tongue, among the filiform papillae. Each has a narrow connective-tissue stalk and a broader top, and taste buds lie in the epithelium lining that top. Because they are rich in capillaries, they show as small red dots on the fresh tongue, and their taste fibres come from the chorda tympani (VII).

The circumvallate papilla is the largest taste papilla, a broad elevation at the back of the tongue lying in front of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis, the groove that marks the boundary between the oral and pharyngeal parts of the tongue. It is encircled by a deep trench, and the walls of that trench hold many taste buds. The ducts of the Von Ebner glands open into the bottom of this trench, so taste buds and duct openings can be seen together in one section.

Foliate papillae are a set of parallel, leaf-like folds of mucosa on the posterolateral margins of the tongue, close to the palatoglossal arch. Narrow clefts (grooves) separate the folds, and taste buds line the walls of these clefts. Von Ebner gland ducts open into the clefts, and their taste fibres come mainly from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

Von Ebner ducts are the short excretory ducts that carry the watery serous secretion from the Von Ebner glands to the surface. They open at the bottom of the trenches around the circumvallate papillae and into the clefts of the foliate papillae, so the secretion can wash over the taste pores. In a section a duct appears as a small open channel lined by epithelium, in contrast to the rounded secretory units it drains.

Filiform papillae are the thread-like, conical projections that occupy the anterior two-thirds of the dorsum of the tongue, and they are the most numerous papillae. They contain no taste buds; their job is mechanical, giving the tongue a rough surface that grips food and moves it around the mouth. Each has a connective-tissue core capped by keratinised epithelium.

The keratinised tips are the cornified caps at the ends of the filiform papillae, made of dead, keratin-filled squamous cells. These cells at the tip are constantly shed and replaced from below, so the tips are continually renewed. Elongation of these filiform tips can produce black hairy tongue, a usually harmless condition.

Gustatory receptor cells are the elongated taste cells in the centre of each taste bud, and they carry the receptors that detect dissolved taste chemicals. Their apical microvilli project through the taste pore to contact food, and in some cells the lower ends form synapses with sensory nerve fibres that carry taste signals to the brain. In a section they are the spindle-shaped cells in the middle of the bud, set apart from the basal cells at its base.

The taste pore is the small opening at the top of each taste bud, where the bud reaches the oral surface. The microvilli, also called taste hairs, are fine finger-like projections from the apical ends of the receptor cells that extend into the pore to meet dissolved food. In a section the pore appears as a narrow notch in the surface epithelium directly above the bud.

Perimysium is the sheet of dense connective tissue that wraps each bundle (fascicle) of skeletal muscle fibres in the tongue, and it carries the blood vessels and nerves that supply them. Interstitial fat is the small amount of fat cells (adipocytes) lying between these bundles. In a section, the perimysium shows as collagen-rich bands separating the muscle fascicles, with fat cells filling the gaps between them.

The superior longitudinal muscle is one of the four intrinsic muscles of the tongue, lying just beneath the dorsal mucosa of the upper surface. Its fibres run along the length of the tongue, so it shortens the tongue and curls the tip upwards. It is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII), and in longitudinal sections its fibres appear as parallel bundles running along the tongue.

The transverse muscle is one of the four intrinsic muscles of the tongue, with fibres that run from the midline fibrous septum out towards the side margins. Because the fibres run across the tongue, their contraction narrows and lengthens it. In a coronal section it is recognised by bundles running horizontally from the midline septum to the sides, and it is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII).

The vertical muscle is one of the four intrinsic muscles of the tongue, with fibres that run from the upper surface down to the underside at the sides of the tongue. Its contraction flattens and broadens the tongue. In a coronal section it appears as bundles running up and down at the lateral parts of the tongue, and it is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII).

The inferior longitudinal muscle is one of the four intrinsic muscles of the tongue, lying along the underside of the tongue just beneath the ventral mucosa. Its fibres run from back to front, so it shortens the tongue and curls the tip downwards. It is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII), and in longitudinal sections it lies in the lower part of the tongue, below the superior longitudinal muscle.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) branch is the lingual branch of cranial nerve IX that supplies the posterior third of the tongue. It carries general sensation and taste from the circumvallate and foliate papillae at the back of the tongue. Its taste fibres relay in the nucleus of the solitary tract in the brainstem before passing on towards the brain.

The lingual nerve, with the chorda tympani joined to it, supplies the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. The lingual nerve itself, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), carries general sensation such as touch, temperature and pain. The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (VII), carries taste from the fungiform papillae and joins the lingual nerve on its way.

The hypoglossal nerve (XII) branch is the motor supply of the tongue, carrying the commands for the intrinsic muscles and most of the extrinsic muscles, including genioglossus and hyoglossus. The palatoglossus is the exception, because it is supplied by the vagus nerve (X). If the hypoglossal nerve is damaged, the tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion when it is protruded.

The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery that runs forward to the tongue, lying deep to the hyoglossus muscle. It supplies the tongue and the floor of the mouth, giving off dorsal lingual branches to the upper surface and a deep lingual artery along the underside. Its dorsal branches supply the mucosa and papillae of the upper surface.

The deep lingual vein drains the underside and deeper parts of the tongue, running along the lower surface close to the lingual frenulum. It joins the lingual vein, which drains into the internal jugular system. On the underside it appears as a blue vessel beneath the mucosa, so it can be identified in a dissection beside the frenulum.

The basement membrane is the thin, specialised layer of extracellular matrix that separates the stratified squamous epithelium from the lamina propria. It is made of a basal lamina (containing laminin and type IV collagen) and a reticular lamina of reticular fibres, and it anchors the epithelium while acting as a selective barrier. In a section it appears as a thin, magenta line at the base of the epithelium with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain.

Basal taste cells are small, rounded, poorly differentiated cells that sit at the base of each taste bud, on the basement membrane. They act as stem cells, dividing and maturing into the receptor and supporting cells that replace the taste cells lost at the surface. In a section they appear as small cells with round nuclei clustered at the bottom of the bud.

Taste cell nuclei are the nuclei of the elongated taste cells that make up each taste bud. In a section they lie in the central part of the bud, at several different heights, so the bud shows as a compact oval group of nuclei within the surface epithelium. The nuclei of the basal cells sit lower, close to the basement membrane.

Serous acinar nuclei are the nuclei of the serous secretory cells that form the acini (rounded secretory units) of the Von Ebner glands. Each nucleus is round and sits towards the base of its cell, away from the lumen where the watery secretion is released. In a section the nuclei form clusters around small acinar lumens, which helps identify the gland tissue.

Interstitial adipocytes are fat cells (adipocytes) scattered in the connective tissue between the bundles of intrinsic tongue muscle. Each is a unilocular fat cell, holding one large lipid droplet that pushes its cytoplasm and flattened nucleus into a thin rim at the edge. In a section they appear as clear, empty-looking rounded spaces among the muscle fibres, with the nucleus pressed against the cell edge.

Squamous epithelial cells are the cells that make up the stratified squamous epithelium lining the tongue. Basal cells are cuboidal or columnar and sit on the basement membrane, and as cells move towards the surface they become progressively flatter. The most superficial cells are flattened sheets, and over the filiform papillae they lose their nuclei and become keratinised.

Squamous epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the cells in the stratified squamous epithelium. Basal and intermediate cells have round to oval nuclei, which flatten and become smaller and denser as the cells rise towards the surface. In keratinised areas the outermost layer is anucleate, meaning it has no nuclei left at all.

Taste cells are the specialised epithelial cells that make up each taste bud. They fall into four types: supporting (type I) cells that give the bud its structure, receptor (type II) cells that detect sweet, bitter and umami chemicals, type III cells that form synapses with nerve fibres, and basal cells that act as stem cells. Their microvilli (taste hairs) reach the taste pore, and the cells are constantly renewed.

Intramuscular connective tissue is the collagen-rich framework that lies inside a muscle, separating and binding its fibres. It forms the endomysium around each muscle fibre and the perimysium around each bundle (fascicle), and it carries the blood vessels and nerves to the fibres. Because its collagen is tough, it transmits the force of contraction from the muscle fibres to the tendon.

The foliate papillae epithelium is the non-keratinised stratified squamous lining of the folds and clefts on the posterolateral margins of the tongue. Taste buds sit in the walls of each cleft, and the Von Ebner gland ducts open at the bottom of the clefts. In a section the taste buds show as barrel-shaped profiles in the cleft walls.

The stroma of the mucosa is the supporting connective-tissue framework beneath the surface epithelium, made of collagen and elastic fibres, fibroblasts and small blood vessels. On the tongue it is the lamina propria, which rises into the papillae as connective tissue cores. In a section it is the fibrous layer that supports the epithelium above and carries the capillaries that feed it.

The circumvallate papilla's trench epithelium is the non-keratinised stratified squamous lining of the moat around the circumvallate papilla. Taste buds lie in the walls of this trench, and the Von Ebner gland ducts open into its floor. Its non-keratinised surface contrasts with the keratinised tips of the nearby filiform papillae.
